steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Systematic fault finding follows a logical sequence: observe symptoms, identify the section at fault, locate the faulty component, then repair and test.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The half-split method tests at the midpoint of a signal path, halving the suspect area with each measurement.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: An open circuit breaks the current path; symptoms include zero current flow and full supply voltage across the break.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A short circuit provides a zero-resistance path; symptoms include excessive current, blown fuses and overheating.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Describe the half-split method of fault finding. | Q: What are the symptoms of an open-circuit resistor in a series circuit? | Q: What is a solder bridge and how can it be detected?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Measure at the midpoint of the signal path; if the signal is correct there, the fault is after that point; if not, it is before. Repeat to narrow down the fault location. | Zero current flows, the full supply voltage appears across the open resistor, and components after the break have no voltage across them. | A solder bridge is an unintended solder connection between adjacent tracks; it is detected by visual inspection and continuity testing with a multimeter.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always describe a systematic approach: observe, identify the section, locate the component, repair, retest. State that the power supply should be checked before signal paths. Explain the half-split method step by step with a practical example. Distinguish clearly between open-circuit symptoms (no current, voltage across break) and short-circuit symptoms (excess current, near-zero voltage across short). Mention both visual inspection and meter testing as complementary fault-finding techniques.
